about: Words for the chain saga_northumbria_irish_sea, 'The saint on the road' (cards: Data/encounters/chain_saga_northumbria_irish_sea_793.json; page: Design/content/chains/saga_northumbria_irish_sea.md). Saint Cuthbert's body carried from Lindisfarne before Halfdan's army, 875 to 883: the Tyne camp, Dublin, Hi, the storm off the Derwent, the book on the Whithorn sands, the slave boy made king. Keys: chain_saga_northumbria_irish_sea.<card>.<what>; an option's label is opt_<key> and its outcome out_<key> (out_<key>_fail for a failed chance); art.<card id> says what the card's picture shows. No words are quoted from any source: the dream, the storm and the grant are told in our own words after the Historia de Sancto Cuthberto and Symeon. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: Halfdan, who shared out the Northumbrians' land, was driven out by his own army. He left the Tyne with three ships and was killed in Ireland, at Strangford Lough, fighting other Northmen.
Saint Cuthbert's people are at Crayke, north of York, after seven years on the road. Their abbot says the saint has named a king for the army: a slave boy at Whittingham.

The army at York and the English have one king: Guthred, Harthacnut's son, bought free from a widow. He has given Saint Cuthbert the land between Tyne and Wear, and thirty-seven days' peace to any who flee to the body.
Saint Cuthbert's body is in Ireland, carried over from the Derwent's mouth in a merchant's hull. The north of England has lost its saint, and says who took him.
The army at York has taken a king of its own kind. The boy the abbot of Carlisle dreamed of would not be bought, and Saint Cuthbert's people are still guests at Crayke.
The island empties
On the holy island the church door stands open and a coffin of carved oak is on a cart in the yard. Monks are loading books. Nobody is singing.
We are taking him off the island. Halfdan is on the Tyne with a fleet, and he does not stop at rivers.
Jarrow and Wearmouth had walls and brothers too. I am from Carlisle. I have seen what is left of a place when they have been.
Two hundred and forty-one years since Aidan came here from Hi. I had hoped to be the bishop who did nothing worth writing down.
The cart can cross the sands at the ebb. The coffin I would rather not trust to a cart on wet sand. You have a boat.
He points at the coffin, at your hull, at the far shore, and then holds up one finger: one tide.
Take the coffin and the books over the water on your hull, at the top of the tide
Buy what they cannot carry: the wax and the spare parchment, for forty pennies
Give twenty pennies for the road
The coffin comes aboard on six oars laid crosswise. It weighs less than a cask of wine. Seven young men walk it up the far beach on their shoulders, and not one of them looks back at the island.
Four cakes of wax and two bundles of parchment, at a price that would shame you in a good year. The abbot counts your pennies twice and thanks you once.
The bishop puts your pennies in the coffin, beside the saint. Nothing else they own will be guarded half as well.
The rock shuts
Under the rock of Bamburgh a monk is buying barley with a silver spoon. The gate above him is shut, and the reeve has come down to see who else has landed.
The king's word: no coffin inside this gate. A saint is a fine thing until the Danes hear where he is lodged.
You go where the wind goes. Go to the Tyne, count his ships, and see if they are caulking them or hauling them up. Thirty pennies, now.
We need to know the same thing he does, and cannot pay for it. If the Tyne is shut we go west over the hills, to the abbot's country.
You carried him over the water. Hunred says the boat did not even dip. He says that kind of thing about everything, but still.
You have not heard. The island is empty. Saint Cuthbert is on a cart behind seven of us, and I am the one who can count, so I buy the barley.
Take the reeve's thirty pennies to go and count the ships on the Tyne
Go and look at the Tyne for the bearers instead, and take nothing for it
Sell the monk two loads of barley at a good year's price, and keep the spoon out of it
He pays first. 'I do not expect to see you twice,' he says. 'If I do, I shall know the Tyne is worse than I thought.'
The monk writes nothing down. He says he will name you at the third psalm of every night office, which is when he is most awake.
Fourteen pennies, counted out of a purse that was once a bishop's glove. He keeps the spoon. It has a dead man's name scratched on the handle.
Halfdan's winter
The Tyne is full of long ships drawn up side by side, under a church with no roof. A Dane has spread altar silver on a sail, and beside it stands a boy with a rope on his wrist.
Count them if you like. The English send someone every week. We are staying the winter, so the number will not change.
Two cups, a plate, the cover off a book. I sell by weight. What it was for is your business.
My lady at Whittingham wants a boy for the geese. Twenty pennies. He looks as if he eats.
Harthacnut's son. His father is dead and so are his father's friends, which makes him cheap. Thirty and he is the widow's. More, and he is yours.
Guthred. I can row.
He holds up a cup, then a weight, then closes his fist: silver for silver. For the boy he opens his hand four times.
Buy the altar silver back by weight: ninety pennies
Outbid the widow's man for the boy: forty pennies
Sell the camp two casks of Rhine wine and ask nothing about the silver
Count the ships, eat his fish, and go
Two cups and a plate, bent to fit a sack. On the foot of one cup somebody has scratched a cross and a name. The Dane throws in the sack.
The widow's man shrugs and goes to look at a cheaper boy. Yours climbs aboard without being told, finds the bailer, and starts using it.
They pay in cut silver, one piece of it still shaped like the arm of a cross. The wine is drunk before you have cast off.
Smoked salmon, and no questions about whose man you are. You count the ships twice and get two numbers. They are not caulking. They mean to stay, and they are dry: wine would sell here.
Three ships
At the ship-fort on the black pool a mail coat and a king's saddle are for sale on the strand. A Dane with a new scar is sitting on the saddle.
Albann, we called him. He came into Loch Cuan with three ships to be a king here. Three ships. He got a mound by the water instead.
The merchant who ate my fish on the Tyne. I had a king then. I have his saddle now.
You are from the east side. So was I. Two winters ago I had a king on the Tyne. I have his saddle now.
The English priests say he went mad and stank, and that is why we drove him out. He did stink. That was not why.
At York they are sharing out the land by the rope. A man who is not there gets the bog. I need to be there.
Carry him home to the Humber for his word and nothing else
Hire him for thirty pennies: he knows this sea from the Liffey to the Solway
Buy him a drink and take the news east
He rows without being asked and sleeps on the saddle. Off the Humber he says: 'When you want a thing said in the army's hall, I will say it.' Then he walks north.
He takes your thirty pennies and the steering oar on the same day. He knows where the Solway dries and how the tide sets off Man. He does not explain. He points.
He drinks, and tells it once more for the cup. Before you go he says the fort is short of wine and grain, and has plenty of everything it stole.
Columba's shrine
On the white strand of Hi a shrine of yew and bronze is being lashed into a hide boat. The abbot watches it go as a man watches his own roof carried off.
It goes to Ireland today, with its keepers. The foreigners have left us our lives twice. I will not ask it of them a third time for a box of bronze.
They say Cuthbert of the English is on the road as well. Aidan went from this strand to that island, and some of Aidan is in that coffin. So the coffin is partly ours.
I have written to their bishop. There is a house for them in Ireland with Columba's people, if they can come to it. I have no one going east. You go everywhere.
We have a verse for nights like the last one. The wind is rough, so the sea-kings stay at home. We pray for bad weather here. It is the one prayer that is often granted.
You took him off the island in your own boat? Then you are in the story already. You may as well carry the letter.
Take the abbot's letter for Bishop Eardulf, wherever he is
Take two of the shrine's keepers and their baggage over to the Irish shore
Sell them a cask for the Mass, against an arm-ring by weight
A folded skin, sealed with a thumb in wax. A brother copies you the verse about the wind on a scrap, in Irish letters, and explains it twice.
Two quiet men and a load they will not let you lift. On the Irish shore they give you a psalter the size of your hand. 'It is all we have that a Saxon would call money.'
The arm-ring weighs out at ninety pennies and a little over. The abbot waves the little away.
The waste city
Legacaestir: Roman walls with ash trees growing out of them and six roofs by the landing. A thin monk has been asking every hull on the Dee the same question.
Franco. My grandfather came over for wool, they say, and stayed for a woman. I carry a dead bishop for a living one.
We mean to take him to Ireland. The bishop has told only the old ones. North of here a river called the Derwent meets the sea. We need a keel there before the new moon.
Last week we were nine men with a salted horse's head and one cheese, and somebody stole the cheese. You see how it is with us.
A letter from Hi? Then there is somewhere to go to. I had begun to think Ireland was only a direction.
You are the Frisian with the boat. Hunred still talks about the boat.
Promise your hull at the Derwent's mouth before the moon is new
Give him ship's bread for nine and let them find another keel
Tell him what the Irish shore is like now, and promise nothing
He kneels on the landing, which embarrasses everyone. Then he gets up and gives you the marks for the Derwent's mouth, like a man who has been saying them over for a week.
Two sacks of ship's bread. He carries both himself. You hear afterwards that they found a keel, and what came of it.
You tell him: a ship-fort on the Liffey, and men in it who sell monks. He nods. 'The bishop says the same of the Tyne. We shall go all the same.'
Three waves
Off the Derwent's mouth, with the coffin lashed amidships and the people left crying on the sand. The wind has backed into the west and the first big sea has come aboard.
Wind is backing west and the sky is the wrong colour. We can still run back in on this. In an hour we cannot.
We did not tell them we were going. Listen to them. I can hear them from here, and I am a little deaf.
That is the third sea aboard, and look at the bilge. Red. It will be the ballast clay. I am telling the men it is the ballast clay.
The book! The chest has come adrift. Bishop Eadfrith wrote it with his own hand. Do not let me be the abbot who watched it go.
Hi has a house waiting for us. If God wants us in it, this is a strange way to say so.
Put about and run back for the Derwent
Leave the helm to the steersman, put about, and lash the book-chest yourself
Hold on for Ireland
Give Ketil the helm, who knows this sea, and hold on for Ireland
She comes round with her rail under. Something square and bright goes over the side as she heels, and the abbot cries out. On the beach they wade in to their waists to take your line.

You get two turns of rope round the chest and one round your own leg before the next sea. She comes round. The book is dry, the saint is going back to the beach he left, and the abbot has hold of your arm.
The chest slides, takes the skin off your shin and goes through the rail. You see the gold on its cover once, going down green. She comes round without it.
Two days of it. On the third morning there is a low green shore, and a man herding cattle who crosses himself when he sees what you carry. The bishop does not speak until the coffin is on the sand.
She will not lie to it. A sea breaks the rail and the book-chest goes with it. What is left of the day is spent running back to the river you left, with two men bailing and one praying.
Ketil takes her north of the worst of it, round an island he does not name. On the second evening he points at a line of hills. 'Ireland. I was nearly killed near here.' The coffin goes ashore dry.
The low tide
The bearer Hunred has walked four days down the coast to find a boat. He has had a dream, and he tells it like a man reading out a tally.
You were not there. Three great seas, the water red in the ship, and the gospel book gone over the side. We turned back. The people on the beach took us for ghosts.
The saint came to me in my sleep. I am to go to the shore at Whithorn, at the lowest ebb of the moon, and look.
Also there is a bridle hanging on a tree. I am to show it to a red horse, which will come to me, and it will draw the cart. He was quite exact.
They found who took the cheese. The bishop prayed, and a fox came out of the wood carrying it. I do not say the man became the fox. Others say it.
It is three days north by sea, and three weeks by land round the firth. I am asking for the three days.
Take him north to the Whithorn sands and walk the ebb with him
Give him bread for the road and keep to your trade
Tell him what salt water does to a book, and wish him a dry road

At the bottom of the ebb the sea is three miles off and the sand lies like a floor. The book is on it, shut, with its gold on. Inside, the pages are white. Hunred does not seem surprised. On the way back he finds the bridle.
He thanks you and goes north on foot with the loaf under his arm. Three weeks, he said.
'Yes,' he says. 'The abbot said that also. Until I told him about the horse.' He goes north on foot.
Harthacnut's son
The boy you bought on the Tyne can hand, reef and steer, and eats like two men. The steersman has come aft to ask what he is to be called on the tally: thrall, or crew.
He pulls a man's oar and eats a man's food. The crew want to know if he gets a man's share, or if we are carrying him as your goods.
My father was Harthacnut. He had a hall and forty men. Then he had enemies. I do not need it talked about. I only do not want it forgotten.
A ship is better than a goose yard. I would stay, if I were asked. Nobody has asked.
One more thing. Half the men will not share a bowl with a heathen in Lent. I only report it.
Free him before the crew, with a share like any man's
Free him, and stand godfather to him at the next church: ten pennies for the white cloth
Sell him on: the widow at Whittingham still wants a boy
You say it at the mast with the crew for witnesses, the way it is done. He says nothing. Then he goes forward and takes the worst oar without being told.
A priest with a cold does it in a river. He comes up Guthred still: he would not take another name. He keeps the white cloth in his sea-chest, under the fish hooks.
Sixty pennies from the widow's steward, who remembers being outbid. The boy walks up the road to Whittingham behind a cart of geese. The crew are quiet for two days.
The abbot's dream
York has had no king for six winters and the army's great men drink in separate halls. Abbot Eadred has come in from Crayke to buy lamp oil, and he looks like a man who has stayed awake on purpose.
The saint stood by my bed at Crayke. I am to cross the Tyne to the army and tell them to make a king: Guthred, Harthacnut's son, whom they sold to a widow at Whittingham.
They are to pay her his price, lead him up Oswigesdune at the sixth hour, and put a gold ring on his right arm. I have the dream. I have not got the price.
The book that went over the side is at Crayke. Hunred found it on the sand at Whithorn, where he was told to look. So I have stopped arguing with dreams.
You walked the sand with Hunred. Then you know what I know: when this saint says where a thing is, it is there.
You tied a gospel book to your own leg in a storm. I think you can be told a dream.
A king out of a widow's goose yard, picked by a dead Englishman. It is the best offer we have had in six winters, which tells you about the others.
This one carried me home from Ireland for nothing. If he says the priest is not mad, I will say it louder, in the hall.
Lend the abbot the boy's price, eighty pennies, against the saint's word
Go into the hall and put the dream to the army in their own tongue
Tell him the boy is not at Whittingham. He is on your ship
Hear the dream out and keep your purse shut
Eighty pennies into a sleeve. 'The saint is good for it,' the abbot says. 'He has been dead near two hundred years and has not yet failed to pay.'
They laugh until the ale is finished. Then an old man asks who Harthacnut's enemies were, and whether any of them is still alive, and nobody can name one. That is when they stop laughing.
He looks at you for some time. 'Whittingham,' he says. 'He was quite exact.' Then: 'Do not sail. I shall come to the landing in three days.'
You hear it out. It is a good dream. At the landing they are already saying that the priests at Crayke have found a king somewhere.
The price of a king
The abbot stands on the landing with two of the army's great men behind him. They are all looking at your crewman, who is looking at a rope he has no need to coil.
That is the one. Harthacnut's son. The saint did not say he would be coiling rope, but I know him.
I was told to pay a widow. It seems you are the widow. What is his price?
I am his to sell. I have known that every day since the Tyne.
I am a free man with a share in this ship. I was sold once. Ask me, not him.
He stood godfather to me. If he says go, I go as from a father's house, not from a market.
Give him up for nothing, and go with him to the hill
Name a king's price: four hundred and eighty pennies, weighed
Say he is a free man with a share in this ship, and let him answer for himself
'Nothing,' you say. The abbot writes it down as if it were a sum. Guthred takes his sea-chest, leaves you the fish hooks, and says: 'A king has a long arm. You will find out how long mine is.'
Two pounds of silver, weighed twice on the army's scales. Guthred watches every piece go into the pan. 'Now I know it to the penny,' he says, and goes ashore without his sea-chest.

'No,' he says, in English, so that the abbot will understand it. 'I have been bought. Once was enough.' The great men look at each other. The abbot looks at the sky, as if something had been left out of the dream.
The gold ring
This year the army and the English together took a king: a young Dane bought out of a widow's yard, with a gold ring on his right arm and the saint's coffin beside him on the hill.
The king has given the saint all the land between the Tyne and the Wear. We are building at Cunecacestre, in the old fort. Seven years on a cart, and he chooses a Roman ditch.
And this: whoever flees to the body has peace for thirty-seven days and nights, from any man, Dane or English. Tell that in your ports. Somebody will need it.
There is the man who had me for forty pennies and let me go for none. Stand by me. I want them to see what an honest price looks like.
The merchant. Four hundred and eighty. I had it weighed again after you left, and it was all there. So we are quits. Exactly quits.
They tell me a Frisian was mixed up in this somewhere. I was minding geese, so I did not see. Was it you?
Eighty pennies you lent the saint. He has had me count out his answer.
You took him off the island on six oars. I remember it. I said then that I hoped to do nothing worth writing down.
Take what the king offers the man who gave him up for nothing
Stand among the witnesses as one who lent or spoke, and take the saint's hand for it
Lay the altar silver from the Tyne on the new altar
Ask only the saint's peace for your hull between Tyne and Wear, and the carrying of his first rents

Arm-rings to the weight of fifteen hundred pennies, from the king's own arm and others. A plot on the river at York, the bishop's seal for the Tyne, and a place at the king's table whenever you land. He asks if you still have his fish hooks.
Nine hundred pennies from the king's gift, counted by the abbot. The bishop sets your name in the book among the saint's men and gives you his seal: no toll for your hull between Tyne and Wear.

The cup with the scratched name goes back on an altar. The bishop turns it round and reads the name aloud. It was one of his own priests. Seven hundred pennies, his seal for the Tyne, and a hand's breadth of the cloth that lay on the coffin.
The bishop has land now and no one to carry its wool. Six hundred pennies paid forward, twelve packs of fleeces to find for him, and his seal: no toll for your hull between Tyne and Wear.
Two saints in one house
Cuthbert of the English lies in Ireland now, a day's walk from Columba's shrine, and the bearer who carried him seven years has learned to ask for bread in Irish.
He lies among Columba's people now. Our founder's house sent Aidan to the English, and the English have sent us a bishop back. We consider the account settled.
You carried my letter, and then you carried what answered it. I do not often get to thank the same man twice.
At home the army has shouted for a king of its own kind. Nobody dreamed for them. The land between Tyne and Wear is some Dane's sheep-walk.
And in every port north of the Humber they say a Frisian sold Saint Cuthbert to the Irish. I tell them he was given. They prefer sold.
That Dane of yours, the tall one. The abbot dreamed about a boy like him once, before we sailed. He never did say what it meant.
Take the abbot's protection: his guest on every shore where Columba's word runs
You carried the letter that called them: ask for the abbot's protection, and a strip of the saint's cloth for your house
Ask for no honour: only to be the man who brings the wine for Columba's houses
Take the protection, and swear fellowship here with Harthacnut's son, whom nobody now will come to buy

Eight hundred pennies' weight in arm-rings, the gift of an Irish king who came to see the coffin. And the abbot's word: on any Irish strand you are his guest, with an honour-price like a free man of his own people.
A thousand pennies' weight, the abbot's word, and a strip of the cloth a hand long, sewn into a leather purse. 'Keep it dry,' Hunred says. 'He is used to that now.'
Six hundred pennies' weight on account, and the cellarer's hand on it: twelve casks before next Easter, and whatever you leave in his store will be there when you come back.
You swear it on the strand, hands on the same oar, with the abbot for witness. Guthred has never heard that he was nearly a king. He is pleased enough to be half of a boat.
Not bought twice
The army at York has shouted for another king, and the saint is still a guest at Crayke. A grey Dane has come down to your hull with a bag of arm-rings for the son of a friend he thought was dead.
His father and I shared a bench. We thought the boy was dead. These are his father's rings, and some of mine, for shame.
The army took another man in the end. He is loud. The priests at Crayke say the saint is displeased. The saint may be right.
They wanted to put a gold ring on my arm and stand me on a hill beside a coffin. I have been stood up to be looked at before. Once.
I would rather have half a boat than all of York. Put my silver with yours. Two hulls, one purse. That is how my people do it.
And you are my godfather, so you cannot cheat me. It is a great saving on witnesses.
Swear fellowship: his kin's silver buys a second hull, and he sails it
Take him into the house as a foster-son, with his kin's gift for his keeping
Send him to York with his rings and your good word, and ask a plot on the river from his kin
Hands on the same purse, before the crew. Seven hundred pennies' weight is your half. In spring there is a second hull, with a Dane at her helm who counts everything and steals nothing.
His kinsman pays nine hundred pennies' weight for his keeping, as for a great man's son. From now on there are Danes at York who call your house kin, and mean it.
He goes up the Ouse in a new cloak. Six hundred pennies' weight is his thanks, and by midsummer a plot on the river at York is staked out in your name, beside his kin's.

Lindisfarne at low water on a grey morning. In front, seven young monks lift a carved oak coffin onto oars laid across a small boat; behind them an old bishop holds a book to his chest, and the church door stands open on an empty nave.

The beach under the rock of Bamburgh, midday, a hard wind. A monk holds out a silver spoon to a man with a barley sack; above them a timber gate is shut, and a reeve in a good cloak comes down the path.

The Tyne in winter dusk. Long ships drawn up side by side on the mud under a church with no roof; in front a Dane sits by a sail spread with bent altar cups, and a boy of twelve stands with a rope on his wrist, looking at the viewer.

The ship-fort at Dublin, a wet afternoon. A turf bank and beached ships behind; in front a scarred Dane sits on a fine saddle laid on the shingle, a mail coat folded beside him, a shipmaster standing over him with a cup.

The white strand of Iona in clear morning light. Two monks lash a house-shaped shrine of wood and bronze into a hide boat; an old abbot stands apart with his hands in his sleeves, and a tall stone cross rises behind him.

Chester from the river, evening. Broken Roman walls with ash trees growing from them, a few thatched roofs by a mud landing; a thin monk with a staff stands at the water's edge, speaking up to a man on a boat.

A small open boat in a green breaking sea under a dark western sky. A coffin is lashed amidships, an old bishop kneels with his hand on it, an abbot reaches after a sliding chest, and the water in the bottom of the boat is red.

Wide wet sands at the lowest ebb, early light, the sea a thin line far off. A young monk bends over a closed book lying on the sand, its gold cover bright; a merchant's boat is aground behind him, tilted on her bilge.
On board at anchor, evening. A tall fair youth of sixteen sits on a thwart mending a net and does not look up; the steersman stands aft by the steering oar with a tally stick, waiting for an answer.

The landing at York below old Roman walls, a dull morning. A tired abbot with an oil jar speaks with his hand raised; behind him a broad Dane in a fur cloak laughs with his head back, and a scarred man watches from a doorway.

A river landing, bright noon. An abbot and two Danish lords stand in a row on the planks, all looking at a young crewman in the boat who coils a rope with his eyes down; the merchant stands between them with empty hands.

A bare hilltop at midday. A young Dane holds up his right arm with a gold ring on it; beside him stands a carved coffin on a cart, a bishop with his hand on the lid, and below them two crowds, Danes with shields and English with staves, standing together.

An Irish monastery yard, soft rain. Small stone huts and a high cross; in front a carved English coffin rests on trestles under a thatched shelter, an Irish abbot and a young English monk on either side of it, a herd of cattle passing behind.

A quay at sunset. A tall young Dane in sea clothes and the merchant stand with their hands laid on one leather purse; a grey-haired Dane pours arm-rings out of a bag onto a cloak at their feet, and two boats lie side by side behind them.
